Under 49 CFR § 395.3(a), a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle is subject to three limits:

1. **Off-duty time required before driving:** 10 consecutive hours off duty (§ 395.3(a)(1)).
2. **On-duty window:** the driver may not drive after the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty following that 10-hour break (§ 395.3(a)(2)).
3. **Driving limit:** a total of 11 hours may be driven within that 14-hour period (§ 395.3(a)(3)(i)).

A related requirement in § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) bars further driving once 8 cumulative hours of driving have passed without an interruption of at least 30 minutes.

These are the long-standing figures from my own knowledge of the regulation rather than a fresh check of the current text, and exceptions elsewhere in Part 395 (such as the sleeper-berth, short-haul, and adverse driving conditions provisions) can modify how they apply.

- **Standard:** "Without unreasonable delay" is the governing test for when the individual notice must go out.
- **Outer limit:** Sixty calendar days is the absolute ceiling.
- **Trigger:** Discovery of the breach starts the 60-day clock, not the date the breach occurred.

The one exception is a law-enforcement delay under § 164.412. An instruction from a law enforcement official temporarily holds back the notice, and HHS reads that as tolling the deadline.

The 60 days is a ceiling, not a safe harbor: an entity that could reasonably have notified sooner can violate the standard even inside 60 days.

Under 47 CFR § 97.313:

- **General maximum:** No amateur station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding **1.5 kW PEP** (peak envelope power), i.e., 1,500 watts PEP ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-D/section-97.313)).

- **10.10-10.15 MHz segment (30-meter band):** The limit is a transmitter power output of **200 W PEP** under § 97.313(c)(1) ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-D/section-97.313), [law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/47/97.313)).

In both cases the measure is peak envelope power (PEP) at the transmitter output, the highest power level emitted at the output of the transmitter ([hamstudy.org](https://hamstudy.org/browse/E3_2023/G1C)).

Note also that § 97.313(a) requires that a station use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications, regardless of these ceilings ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-D/section-97.313)).

Under 49 CFR § 173.120(a), a Class 3 flammable liquid is a liquid having a flash point of **not more than 60 °C (140 °F)**, i.e., at or below (≤) that temperature [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120).

The definition also covers a second category: any material in a liquid phase with a flash point **at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F)** that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging [law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/173.120).

One of the search results, a University of Illinois summary, lists the threshold as ≤ 60.5 °C (141 °F) [drs.illinois.edu](https://drs.illinois.edu/Page2/Programs/ShippingAndReceivingHazardousMaterials/Definitions). That differs from the regulatory text, which states 60 °C (140 °F), and appears to reflect an older version of the rule. The same page also gives the heated-material criterion as ≤ 37.8 °C, whereas the regulation says at or above 37.8 °C.

Under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), the trigger height is **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level**.

Any employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal or vertical) with an unprotected side or edge at that height must be protected by one of three systems:

- **Guardrail systems**
- **Safety net systems**
- **Personal fall arrest systems**

The employer may choose any of the three; each must meet the criteria in § 1926.502. This is the general construction-industry rule, and other paragraphs of § 1926.501(b) set specific requirements for particular situations such as leading edges, hoist areas, holes, and roofing work.

Under 29 CFR § 825.200(a), an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to **a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period** [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-C/part-825/subpart-B/section-825.200).

That 12-workweek total applies to any one or more of the following qualifying reasons [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-C/part-825/subpart-B/section-825.200):

1. The birth of the employee's son or daughter, and to care for the newborn child
2. The placement of a son or daughter with the employee for adoption or foster care, and to care for the newly placed child
3. To care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition
4. A serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform one or more of the essential functions of their job
5. Any qualifying exigency arising from the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent being a military member on covered active duty (or notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty)

The employer may choose how the 12-month period is measured: the calendar year, another fixed 12-month leave year, a 12-month period measured forward from the employee's first FMLA leave, or a "rolling" 12-month period measured backward from the date leave is used [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-C/part-825/subpart-B/section-825.200).

The excluded category, leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, has a separate limit of 26 workweeks during a single 12-month period [law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/825.200).

**Text line: 1000 octets. Reply line: 512 octets.** Both counts include the terminating CRLF.

- **Text line (4.5.3.1.6):** The 1000-octet figure counts the two-octet CRLF, so you get 998 octets of actual content per line ([emailmarketing.net](https://emailmarketing.net/learn/rfc/rfc5321-smtp)). PHPMailer encodes the same reading, setting its maximum line length constant to 998 "*excluding* a trailing CRLF break" ([github.com](https://github.com/PHPMailer/PHPMailer/blob/640e68d33218e9886ec700b058613d5552cb31fe/src/SMTP.php)). Its code comments also note that the extra leading dot added for transparency (dot-stuffing) sits outside that count.

- **Reply line (4.5.3.1.5):** The 512 octets cover the reply code as well as the CRLF ([emailmarketing.net](https://emailmarketing.net/learn/rfc/rfc5321-smtp)).

Two caveats:

- Section 4.5.3.1 frames these as sizes every implementation must be able to handle, which is why the summary table labels them a "Minimum capacity" ([emailmarketing.net](https://emailmarketing.net/learn/rfc/rfc5321-smtp)). In practice senders treat them as maximums, since anything longer is not guaranteed to be accepted.
- SMTP service extensions are allowed to alter the limits in Section 4.5.3 ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321.html)).

The search results included only the table of contents for these subsections, not their full text, so the details above rest on a secondary summary and PHPMailer's source comments.

Workers in Great Britain are entitled by statute to **5.6 weeks** of paid annual leave per year, **capped at 28 days** [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights).

A few key points:

- **How it's calculated:** For someone working a full leave year, the entitlement is the lower of 28 days or 5.6 × the number of days worked per week [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/calculating-holiday-entitlement-for-workers/how-to-calculate-holiday-entitlement-for-workers-on-different-types-of-contract). So a 5-day-a-week worker gets 28 days, while someone working 3 days a week gets at least 16.8 days [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights).
- **When the cap bites:** In practice, the cap only affects people who work more than 5 days a week [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/calculating-holiday-entitlement-for-workers/how-to-calculate-holiday-entitlement-for-workers-on-different-types-of-contract). For example, staff working 6 days a week are still only entitled to 28 days [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights).
- **Bank holidays:** These do not have to be given as paid leave, but an employer can choose to count them as part of the statutory entitlement [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights).
- **Irregular-hours and part-year workers:** For leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024, their holiday accrues at 12.07% of actual hours worked in a pay period [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/simplifying-holiday-entitlement-and-holiday-pay-calculations/holiday-pay-and-entitlement-reforms-from-1-january-2024).

This is the legal minimum. Employers can offer more through the contract, but not less [london.gov.uk](https://www.london.gov.uk/programmes-strategies/communities-and-social-justice/employment-rights-hub/time-and-leave).

Under 14 CFR 91.155, the basic VFR weather minimums in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL are:

- **Flight visibility:** 3 statute miles
- **Distance from clouds:**
  - 500 feet below
  - 1,000 feet above
  - 2,000 feet horizontal

A common memory aid is "3-152" (3 SM, 1,000 above, 500 below, 2,000 horizontal).

For comparison, at or above 10,000 feet MSL in Class E the minimums increase to 5 statute miles visibility, with 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 1 statute mile horizontal from clouds.

In the original DNS specification (RFC 1035, November 1987), the size limits are:

- **Labels:** 63 octets or less
- **Full domain names:** 255 octets or less

These are listed in section 2.3.4, "Size limits" [rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc1035/).

**Why these limits exist:**

- The label limit comes from the wire format: each label is preceded by a one-octet length field, and the high-order two bits of that octet must be zero, so the remaining six bits limit the label to 63 octets or less [rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc1035/).
- The 255-octet name limit was imposed "to simplify implementations," and it counts both the label octets and the label length octets [rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc1035/).

RFC 2181, which clarifies the specification, restates these limits: a label is between 1 and 63 octets, and a full domain name is limited to 255 octets including the separators [rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2181.html).

Under OSHA's respirable crystalline silica standard for general industry and maritime (29 CFR § 1910.1053):

- **Permissible exposure limit (PEL): 50 µg/m³**, calculated as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA). Employers must ensure no employee is exposed above this level [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1053).
- **Action level (AL): 25 µg/m³**, also calculated as an 8-hour TWA [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1053).

**What these limits trigger:**

- **Exposure assessment:** Employers must assess the exposure of each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level [osha.gov](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3911.pdf).
- **Medical surveillance:** Since June 23, 2020, this requirement is triggered by exposures at or above the action level for 30 or more days per year [osha.gov](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/enforcement/directives/CPL_02-02-080.pdf).
- **Exemption:** The standard does not apply where the employer has objective data showing exposures will remain below 25 µg/m³ as an 8-hour TWA under any foreseeable conditions [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1053).

**Other details:**

- The limits apply to the three covered forms of crystalline silica: quartz, cristobalite, and tridymite [osha.gov](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/enforcement/directives/CPL_02-02-080.pdf).
- Employee exposure is defined as the exposure that would occur if the employee were not using a respirator [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1053).
- Because both limits are 8-hour averages, exposures can fluctuate during a shift as long as the average stays within the limit [osha.gov](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3911.pdf).
- Most provisions of the standard became enforceable on June 23, 2018 [osha.gov](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2018-06-07).

The 1876 Pocket Manual requires a **two-thirds vote** to adopt the Previous Question.

Section 20 states that the motion "is not debatable, and cannot be amended or have any other Subsidiary motion applied to it. It shall require a two-thirds vote for its adoption." [gutenberg.pglaf.org](https://gutenberg.pglaf.org/9/0/9/9097/9097-h/9097-h.htm)

A few related points from the same text:

- **Rationale:** Robert explains that "in ordinary assemblies it is rarely expedient to deprive a large minority of the right of debate, and yet two-thirds of the members should have the right to close the debate when they think it best." [gutenberg.pglaf.org](https://gutenberg.pglaf.org/9/0/9/9097/9097-h/9097-h.htm)
- **Contrast with Congress:** The manual notes that the motion "requires only a majority vote for its adoption in the House of Representatives, and is not allowed in the United States Senate." Robert describes his two-thirds rule as "a mean between those of the House and Senate." [gutenberg.pglaf.org](https://gutenberg.pglaf.org/9/0/9/9097/9097-h/9097-h.htm)
- **Consistency elsewhere in the manual:** Section 37 on closing debate likewise says the motions that cut off debate, except to Lie on the Table, "shall require a two-thirds vote for their adoption." [gutenberg.pglaf.org](https://gutenberg.pglaf.org/9/0/9/9097/9097-h/9097-h.htm)

This is the edition Project Gutenberg carries as eBook #9097, the original published by S. C. Griggs & Company in Chicago in 1876. [gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9097)

In the 9th edition of the SI Brochure, the luminous efficacy K<sub>cd</sub> is fixed at **683 lm/W** for monochromatic radiation of frequency **540 × 10¹² Hz** [bipm.org](https://www.bipm.org/en/-/resolution-cgpm-26-1).

This fixed value defines the candela: K<sub>cd</sub> is taken to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹, which is equal to cd sr W⁻¹, or cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ [nist.gov](https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/si-units-luminous-intensity). Like the other six defining constants of the SI, this numerical value is exact and has no uncertainty [nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.330-2019.pdf).

In practical terms, one candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W/sr [nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.330-2019.pdf).

None. 14 CFR § 91.151 sets no fuel reserve for gliders, because the rule only covers airplanes and rotorcraft.

The VFR fuel reserves it does set are:

- **Airplanes, day:** enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, fly 30 minutes beyond it.
- **Airplanes, night:** the same, but 45 minutes beyond it.
- **Rotorcraft:** enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and fly 20 minutes beyond it at normal cruising speed.

This also means a motorglider or self-launching glider, which is certificated in the glider category, has no VFR fuel reserve under this section. The pilot is still bound by the general duties in § 91.103 (preflight planning, including fuel requirements) and § 91.13 (careless or reckless operation).

No, it is not a Class 3 flammable liquid. It is a **combustible liquid**.

**Why it is not Class 3:** Under 49 CFR 173.120(a), a flammable liquid is one with a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F) [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120). At 65 °C (149 °F), your liquid is above that threshold. The only other route into Class 3 is if the liquid is intentionally heated and offered or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, which I am assuming is not the case here.

**Why it is a combustible liquid:** A combustible liquid is any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F) [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120). Your liquid meets both conditions. PHMSA has confirmed that a material in this flash point range that meets no other hazard class definition must be classed as a combustible liquid for domestic transportation, for example as NA1993, Combustible liquid, PG III [phmsa.dot.gov](https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/regulations/title49/interp/14-0058).

**Practical points:**

- **Do not class it up to flammable.** PHMSA says a material meeting the combustible liquid definition should be classed and described as such [phmsa.dot.gov](https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/regulations/title49/interp/14-0058).
- **It may fall outside the regulations entirely.** A combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion, as tested under ASTM D 4206 or appendix H of Part 173, is not subject to the regulations as a combustible liquid [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120).
- **Non-bulk shipments are generally not regulated.** The combustible liquid category is a US domestic one, and combustible liquids in non-bulk packages are generally exempt from regulation when offered by ground [drs.illinois.edu](https://drs.illinois.edu/Page2/Programs/ShippingAndReceivingHazardousMaterials/Definitions).

Some secondary sources, such as [safer.fmcsa.dot.gov](https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/mcmisfile/hm_div_3_comb-liq.htm), still show an older 60.5 °C (141 °F) threshold. The current regulation uses 60 °C, and the difference does not affect a 65 °C liquid.

The limits are in 10 CFR 20.1301(a):

- **Per year:** 0.1 rem (1 mSv) is the annual ceiling on total effective dose equivalent that a member of the public may receive from a licensed operation.
- **In any one hour, unrestricted area:** 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) caps the external-source dose in an unrestricted area over any single hour.

The annual figure leaves out certain contributions: background radiation, the person's own medical administrations, exposure to released patients, voluntary medical research participation, and the licensee's permitted sanitary sewer disposal are all left out of the tally.

One exception: with prior NRC authorization, a licensee or applicant can be allowed an annual public limit as high as 0.5 rem (5 mSv).

The search results show the standard text of the rule but don't confirm whether it has been amended very recently, so check the current eCFR if you need this for compliance.

**Annual: 9.0 µg/m³. 24-hour: 35 µg/m³.**

- **Annual (primary):** A February 7, 2024 rule cut this level to 9.0 µg/m³ from the previous 12.0 µg/m³. Compliance is judged on the annual mean averaged over three years.
- **24-hour (primary):** The 2024 rule left this level untouched at 35 µg/m³. Its form is the 98th percentile, averaged over three years.

The 2024 annual standard has faced a court challenge and an EPA reconsideration. The most recent source I found (about three months old) still lists 9.0 µg/m³, but EPA's NAAQS table is the place to confirm nothing has changed since.

**20 minutes.** Under 14 CFR § 91.151(b), a rotorcraft may not begin a VFR flight unless, considering wind and forecast weather, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, at normal cruising speed, for at least 20 more minutes.

This is from memory rather than a fresh lookup, though the rule has been stable for decades. For comparison, airplanes need 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night. Commercial operators may have stricter requirements under their own rules or operations specifications.

From 1 April 2026 the rates are:

- **National Living Wage (21 and over):** £12.71 an hour, a 50p (4.1%) increase on the previous £12.21.
- **National Minimum Wage (18 to 20):** £10.85 an hour, up 85p (8.5%) from £10.00.

Looking ahead, ministers have confirmed the next uprating for 1 April 2027: £13.21 for the 21-and-over band and £11.27 for 18 to 20 year olds.

**$184,500** caps the earnings on which workers owe Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax in 2026, according to the Social Security Administration.

Workers in 2025 faced a lower cap of $176,100.

Under the short-haul exception in 49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1):

- **Radius:** The driver must operate within a **150 air-mile radius** (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location [ecfr.io](https://ecfr.io/Title-49/Section-395.1).
- **Time limit:** The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within **14 consecutive hours** [ecfr.io](https://ecfr.io/Title-49/Section-395.1).

A driver who meets these conditions is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11, the records of duty status (RODS) and supporting documents rules [fmcsa.dot.gov](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/hours-service/summary-hours-service-regulations).

Two other conditions also apply:

- **Off-duty time:** Property-carrying drivers must have at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty; for passenger-carrying drivers it is 8 hours [ecfr.io](https://ecfr.io/Title-49/Section-395.1).
- **Time records:** The motor carrier must keep accurate time records for 6 months, showing the time the driver reports for duty, the total hours on duty, and the time released each day [ecfr.io](https://ecfr.io/Title-49/Section-395.1).

If the driver goes beyond the distance or time limit on a given day, they must complete a RODS for that day as soon as the exception no longer applies [fmcsa.dot.gov](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/sites/fmcsa.dot.gov/files/2022-04/FMCSA-HOS-395-DRIVERS-GUIDE-TO-HOS%282022-04-28%29_0.pdf).

The limit on employee elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for 2026 is **$24,500**, before any catch-up contributions, according to [irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits). This is up from $23,500 in 2025 ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions)).

A few related details:

- **Lesser-of rule:** The limit is $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-contributions)).
- **Aggregation:** The limit generally applies to the total of all elective deferrals you make across all plans in which you participate ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits)).
- **SIMPLE 401(k) plans:** A lower limit of $17,000 applies for 2026 ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits)).
- **Plan terms:** Your specific plan may impose a lower limit ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits)).
